Title: Stabilizing Quantum-Liouville equations with complex absorbing potentials in discontinuous Galerkin frameworks
Text:
ORIGINAL RESEARCH
Journal of Applied Mathematics and Computing (2025) 71 (Suppl 2):S1711–S1732

Abstract
Efficiently solving quantum transport equations requires numerical methods that 
can handle open boundary conditions while maintaining accuracy and stability. This 
work introduces a novel approach combining the Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) 
method with Complex Absorbing Potentials (CAP) to approximate the Liouville-
von Neumann equation. The DG method is particularly suited for high-performance 
computing, leveraging its block-diagonal matrix structure for parallelization and 
computational efficiency. By integrating CAPs, we mitigate non-physical boundary 
reflections, thereby improving stability and accuracy in both stationary and transient 
regimes. We conduct a rigorous analysis to evaluate how the integration of a CAP 
influences the stability and coercivity of the DG scheme, validating its effectiveness 
through numerical experiments on a resonant tunneling diode. Results demonstrate 
that CAP significantly reduces oscillatory artifacts and stabilizes the DG scheme by 
ensuring the eigenvalue spectrum lies in the left half-plane. This approach provides 
a robust framework for quantum transport simulations in nanoscale devices.

1  Introduction
In the context of nano device simulations, the accurate and efficient solving of trans­
port equations is essential. Where numerical algorithms like the Finite Volume (FV) 
and Finite Difference technique distinguish themselves in terms of computational 
efficiency, they lack in terms of numerical accuracy [1, 2]. Other state-of-the-art 
methods like the Quantum Transmitting Boundary Method [3], Monte Carlo inte­
gration techniques [4] or the Non-Equilibrium Green’s Function [5, 6], on the other 
hand, offer superior numerical accuracy yet suffer from insufficient computational 
efficiency, specifically when considering transient simulations [4, 7, 8].
Quantum transport equations, like for example the Wigner transport equation 
(WTE), Liouville-von Neumann equation (LVNE), and Quantum-Liouville type 
equations (QLTE) have evolved in their usability when simulating electron trans­
port in nanostructure devices [9]. In previous works [10], the discontinuous Galerkin 
(DG) method has been shown to be a promising algorithm to combine numerical 
accuracy and computational efficiency. With its working principle being based on 
matrix-vector multiplication, it is specifically suited for simulations of the ballistic 
regime. Since the DG method operates with block-diagonal matrices, it is also best 
suited to exploit high performance computing paradigms, like parallel computing. In 
theory a block-diagonal matrix can be split into its submatrices and either inverted or 
multiplied with a vector or matrix more efficiently. The sub-results can then be col­
lected into a new vector, potentially decreasing the computation time of a simulation 
by a large margin. Furthermore, as shown in a previous work [11], the DG algorithm 
delivers more accurate results when compared to the FV technique, allowing for a 
more coarse grid and thus reducing the computation time significantly. However, the 
DG method suffers from an inherent disadvantage regarding the numerical flux.
Similar to the FV technique, a numerical flux is deployed to represent the flow of 
information in a given system. In the context of the DG algorithm, the numerical flux 
additionally links the neighboring, otherwise discontinuous, finite elements. Unfor­
tunately, depending on the choice of the numerical flux it can introduce instability 
leading to divergence during time-dependent simulations. To circumvent this issue, 
it has been shown in [12] that utilizing a complex absorbing potential (CAP) reduces 
the instability introduced by the numerical flux of the DG scheme. Although the CAP 
is a well-known method in the field of quantum chemistry, its usage with the WTE or 
LVNE are novel [13–15].
Since most Schroedinger-based transport equations, and the (LVNE) in particular, 
demand an infinitely expanding domain regarding the relative coordinate, a poten­
tial issue can emerge as the numerical approximation requires a finite computational 
domain. A problem arises here when the Wigner transformation is applied onto the 
LVNE to arrive at the Quantum-Liouville type equation (QLTE), which leads to a 
surface term [13]. If the surface term is neglected, the boundaries are terminated with

Furthermore, this work will include a detailed analysis of the CAP with regard to 
the LVNE. Section 2 will cover the fundamentals of the LVNE as well as the CAP 
with the aim to create a self-contained work. In Sect. 3, a novel integration of the 
CAP with the DG approach within the framework of the LVNE will be discussed 
and the coercivity as well as the stability of the numerical scheme will be analyzed. 
Section 4 will present the numerical experiments and Sect. 5 will conclude with the 
essential findings.

2.2  The complex absorbing potential
The role and idea behind the CAP shall be discussed in the following. Its implementa­
tion will be demonstrated in Sect. 4.
To discuss the motivation behind the CAP, one has to understand the physical 
context during quantum transport simulations and specifically what happens at the 
boundaries of the computational domain. Since in the transport direction regarding 
χ the contacts can be found, the discussion of the correct boundary conditions is 
not relevant here and will be discussed at a later point. For the analytical solution of

such that the propagating waves can vanish in infinity [14]. In the bounded compu­
tational domain Ωξ, the interval is defined by [−L/2, +L/2]. When the parameter L 
approaches ∞, the statistical density ρ approaches 0 resulting from the square inte­
grability condition due to the L2-norm [14].

have to be set. To address this problem, there are three commonly used methods. 
Periodic boundary conditions (PBC) [20, 21], open boundary conditions (OBC) [22, 
23], and closed boundary conditions (CBC) [24]. Although PBCs and CBCs are more 
commonly used with the density functional theory it is also feasible to implement

of the open boundary conditions from the interior values of the LVNE for every dis­

pursued further. The next possibility is to formulate a PML based on the Schroedinger 
picture. However, after a transformation of the coordinates, as discussed previously, 
the PML would affect areas inside of the computational domain and, more impor­

not be analyzed any further. Finally, the concept of the CAP originates from the PML,

5  Conclusion
This work has introduced open boundary conditions in the form of a complex absorb­
ing potential to account for the open boundedness of the Liouville-von Neumann 
equation. The CAP was derived by exploiting the symmetries of the LVNE in the 
relative direction. Furthermore, the discontinuous Galerkin method was introduced

scheme was investigated and mathematically proven. Finally, with numerical experi­
ments utilizing a resonant tunneling diode, the effect of the CAP was proven and dis­
played. It was shown, that the CAP indeed suppresses artificial reflections especially 
for the imaginary part of the statistical density ρ. It was further detailed that the CAP 
is able to stabilize the DG method by moving the eigenvalue spectrum to the left in 
the complex plane ensuring stability for transient regimes.

Abstract: Efficiently solving quantum transport equations requires numerical methods that can handle open boundary conditions while maintaining accuracy and stability. This work introduces a novel approach combining the Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method with Complex Absorbing Potentials (CAP) to approximate the Liouville- von Neumann equation. The DG method is particularly suited for high-performance computing, leveraging its block-diagonal matrix structure for parallelization and computational efficiency. By integrating CAPs, we mitigate non-physical boundary reflections, thereby improving stability and accuracy in both stationary and transient regimes. We conduct a rigorous analysis to evaluate how the integration of a CAP influences the stability and coercivity of the DG scheme, validating its effectiveness through numerical experiments on a resonant tunneling diode. Results demonstrate that CAP significantly reduces oscillatory artifacts and stabilizes the DG scheme by ensuring the eigenvalue spectrum lies in the left half-plane. This approach provides a robust framework for quantum transport simulations in nanoscale devices.
